passages.section: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
passages.location: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
passages.text: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor–critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03% vs. 0.63%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.

Online 3D bin packing requires selecting and placing boxes as they arrive, without knowing the complete arrival sequence. In warehouse settings, a small processing buffer allows for limited reordering prior to placement (Fig. 1 ). The objective is to pack densely while keeping the stack stable, which depends on the box dimensions, physics, and the order, orientation, and location of placement.

Physical stability depends on more than the visible top surface. Supporting material properties and the arrangement of multiple supporting boxes can affect a placement’s outcome. One box collapse can leave the bin disorganized and hurt the long-term packing compactness. Therefore, there have been works trying to integrate physics-aware stability information into packing decision making.

Reinforcement learning (RL) packers usually handle stability with an action mask. Most masks are computed using geometric or physics-based rules on the height map or the stacking structure [ 1 , 2 ] . Instead, [ 3 ] and [ 4 ] learn the stability mask through simulation outcomes together with a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) policy [ 5 ] , but apply the masks as hard filters on the placement of a box the policy has already chosen. Stability therefore cannot influence which box to pack, leading to a policy that is not jointly optimal. Moreover, a placement is either allowed or forbidden, with no trade-off between its risk and the volume it adds. This motivates designing a more advanced joint policy in which stability awareness can directly affect selection among boxes, orientations, and placements in the long run.

We propose SHORE, which separates the prediction of the outcome of the current placement from the value of the subsequent packing, but intelligently fuses the stability information back to guide the long-term joint policy learning. A 3D U-Net reads bin occupancy and the oriented box properties to estimate whether the whole stack satisfies the stability test after the placement. A separate action-conditioned critic learns the return if the current placement holds, including its immediate reward and subsequent packing, from on-policy rollouts. The stability estimate modulates this value and provides a soft prior to the joint actions of the actor (Fig. 2 ). In this on-policy actor–critic method, the critic scores every valid (box, orientation, placement) triple, and the actor follows the exact expected gradient over all of them, so the stability estimate shapes which box is packed and how it is turned, not only where it goes. At inference, SHORE chooses each placement with one pass of the actor and of the stability network.
In short, our contributions are:

A physics-aware RL strategy that uses learned placement-stability probabilities as continuous weights on action values for policy improvement over joint box–orientation–placement actions, so that the packing agent can trade the risk of an unstable placement against the volume it adds.
A highly parallel, Isaac Gym-based bin packing environment that enables fast, large-scale on-policy RL training.
An empirical study of the efficiency of this method on a realistic box distribution, together with an initial real-robot deployment test.

Online 3D Bin Packing. This problem setting involves making packing decisions without knowledge of incoming items, leading to unique challenges in achieving optimality and efficiency. The early efforts on this problem are mostly studies about developing adaptive heuristics and algorithms that can handle the sequential nature of item arrivals. For example, [ 6 ] and [ 7 ] utilize deepest-bottom-left (DBL) heuristics, while [ 8 ] introduces Heightmap-Minimization heuristics.

Recent work in this area has moved beyond classical heuristics to incorporate deep learning, physics constraints, and more generalizable models. [ 9 ] use DRL to solve the specific setting with an arbitrary number of bins and any bin size, and show RL + search heuristics outperform traditional online heuristics across a range of instances. [ 10 ] tackle the problem with constrained DRL, framing the problem as a constrained Markov decision process under limited lookahead and enforcing physical stability, and show strong improvements over previous heuristics. [ 11 ] designs a complete robot pipeline to narrow the gap of heuristic DRL framework between simulation and real world. More recently, [ 2 ] introduces a DRL model that not only places items but also generalizes to bins of varying sizes via a transformer architecture that fuses item and bin subspace features. [ 12 ] integrate a physics heuristic with object rearrangement and stable placement into a DRL framework to reduce wasted space and improve utilization. However, the design of good heuristics remains a challenge, which leads to the emergence of learning-based action masking models.

Action masking models. Action masking has emerged as a practical strategy to tackle the enormous, state-dependent action space in the online 3D bin packing setting. [ 13 ] propose a feasibility-prediction module that learns a binary “feasibility mask” over placement choices and uses that mask to modulate actor probabilities during training, which substantially speeds learning and enforces collision/stability constraints. Building on the same idea, [ 14 ] allows custom action-mask definitions including reorientation and empty maximal spaces (EMSs), and compares masking strategies with search-based planners. [ 1 ] instead compute the feasibility mask for the placement actions based on the stacking tree analysis. [ 4 ] incorporate physics properties into the mask calculation to improve sample efficiency and reduce unsafe actions during exploration. [ 2 ] uses pairwise action-masking between EMSs and orientations to guarantee that the policy only samples pairs, further improving generalization in the online setting. [ 3 ] learn the mask online from physics simulations, jointly with the policy. All of these masks are hard filters on placements. SHORE instead keeps a geometric mask only for fit and support, and uses a learned stability probability inside the action value, where it can be traded against packed volume and affects which box is packed.

An episode ends in one of three ways: (i) completion , when every box in the sequence has been placed; (ii) infeasibility , when the method’s feasibility filter admits no placement for the next decision; and (iii) instability , when an executed placement violates Eq. ( 2 ). For SHORE, GOPT+ and GOPT, the feasibility filter is purely geometric: it is the rule-based mask m ⁡ ( s , a ) m(s,a) of Sec. SHORE and GOPT+ apply it to every visible box in every orientation, so an infeasible ending means that no visible box fits anywhere with enough support; GOPT applies it only to the buffer head in its stored orientation. For OL Mask, the filter of the selected box also includes the learned stability mask, so its episodes can also end when the mask rejects every placement as unstable. An infeasible ending can therefore mean that no box fits in the remaining space, or that the filter rejects placements that would in fact be stable, and the evaluation does not separate the two.

The stability model addresses a specific weakness of the plain learner. A collapse pays 0 and ends the episode, so a plain critic must learn, for every action, the product of two different quantities: the chance that the placement holds, which depends on the densities and support under the footprint, and the value of the packing that follows. A label is the binary outcome of a placement, y = 1 y=1 if it held and y = 0 y=0 if it collapsed, stored with its state in a buffer 𝒟 S \mathcal{D}_{S} . Executed placements. Every placement executed in a rollout is labeled by its real outcome, with label weight ζ = 2 \zeta=2 . A random 10% of executed outcomes go to a holdout set, excluded from supervised training and used to assess the learning copy S ψ S_{\psi} before activation (Sec. IV-G ).

The critic, the label buffer and the simulator are used only during training. At deployment, SHORE computes the geometric mask, one actor pass and the stability network’s passes for the visible items. It then executes arg ⁡ max a ∈ 𝒜 ⁡ ( s ) ​ [ ℓ θ ​ ( s , a ) + w π ​ log ⁡ S ~ ​ ( s , a ) ] \arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}(s)}[\ell_{\theta}(s,a)+w_{\pi}\log\widetilde{S}(s,a)] , the mode of Eq. ( 9 ). No search is run and no placement is simulated.
The experiments answer three questions:
Does explicit stability modeling accelerate policy learning and improve the trade-off between packed volume and collapse risk, beyond the benefit of buffer selection and rotation?
Where must the stability estimate act: in the critic, in the policy, or in both?
Do simulated stability labels help beyond the labels of executed placements, and is choosing them by uncertainty better than choosing them at random?

All methods share the simulator, box sets, stability criterion (Eq. ( 2 )) and evaluation protocol (Sec. V-C ). The baselines keep their own action spaces and rewards. Except where stated, they place every box in its stored orientation, as in their original implementations, while SHORE and GOPT+ choose among six orientations.

Masked-PPO variants. OL Mask [ 3 ] learns a stability mask online from physics simulations, jointly with a PPO policy. It is the strongest prior method in this setting and the closest to ours, since it also learns stability from physics. Nomask removes masking entirely. Random Selection randomly picks the box from the buffer with only the placement decided by the policy network; Random Placement places at random positions with only box selection determined by the policy.

Learning-based state of the art. GOPT [ 2 ] is a transformer-based DRL packer using Empty Maximal Spaces (EMSs — the maximal axis-aligned empty boxes remaining in the bin) as placement candidates. We use the official implementation (Packing Transformer, EMS placement generator, and masked PPO) and swap only its geometric environment for ours, so that placements are executed and adjudicated by the same physics: unstable placements terminate episodes exactly as for the other methods. Since GOPT is a strict online packer without buffer selection, it packs the buffer head at each step. GOPT+ extends GOPT to the action space of SHORE. The same Packing Transformer chooses any visible box in any of its six orientations, i.e., a joint (box, orientation, EMS) action, and is trained with GOPT’s masked PPO [ 5 ] , with the clipped ratio applied separately to the (box, orientation) choice and to the EMS choice. Its rollout size, learning rate and number of updates are matched to SHORE − - actor prior − - critic weighting, so GOPT+ has the actor network and the action space of SHORE − - actor prior − - critic weighting and differs from it in the learner.

We run all training and evaluation in Isaac Gym [ 20 ] with the GPU-accelerated PhysX backend. A placement is executed as a release 2 2 mm above the target position in the selected orientation, without a full arm trajectory or added Gaussian position or rotation perturbations. This deliberate simplification keeps the property that matters for the decision problem, whether the stack holds, while abstracting away manipulator dynamics. A single box released on the bin settles onto its target with zero measurable drift.

For sim-to-sim transfer, we calibrated Isaac Gym’s PhysX contact behavior against high-fidelity MuJoCo using paired placement replays (Appendix A ). This aligns the faster simulator with MuJoCo’s placement outcomes while retaining Isaac Gym’s GPU-parallel capacity for large-scale RL training. Agreement is high but imperfect, so reported results remain specific to the calibrated Isaac Gym model.

In implementation, the bin is 25 × 25 25\times 25 cm with a maximum stacking height of 20 20 cm, discretized into 25 × 25 × 20 25\times 25\times 20 voxels of 1 1 cm for placement choice. The length of the processing buffer is set to 5. Our box configuration uses light and heavy densities of 100 100 and 5000 5000 kg/m 3 , respectively, following the released implementation of [ 3 ] . This density contrast makes density-aware ordering important. Four types of boxes with different dimensions (length, width, and height), densities, and rigidities are used. While the density parameter controls how heavy the box is, the rigidity parameter controls the deformation degree of the box under contact forces; both impact placement stability. The detailed box specification is listed in Tab. I . The mixture of light deformable and heavy rigid boxes is what makes stability depend on more than geometry: for example, packing the light 6 × 6 × 4 6\times 6\times 4 boxes first produces a soft top surface, and any heavy 8 × 6 × 6 8\times 6\times 6 box arriving later must either be placed on that yielding surface (typically unstable) or terminate the episode. A policy that knows which surfaces will hold can choose its boxes and placements to keep rigid support available.

The total volume of all boxes in the base set is 0.691 0.691 of the bin volume, which caps utilization even if every box is packed successfully. This near-saturation ceiling makes the base set a weak test of further packing gains. We therefore also evaluate on the expanded FBA set, whose broader range of 12 carton dimensions better represents varied fulfillment-box sizes and raises the all-boxes-packed ceiling to 0.866 0.866 . The expanded set offers more headroom for comparing packing strategies and makes box choice and orientation more consequential. The base set remains useful for checking whether the method’s behavior transfers to a simpler, nearly saturated inventory.

Completion rate and unstable rate report the fractions of episodes that end with every box placed and with a collapse (Sec. III-E ). We do not report the share of infeasible endings as a metric: what it measures depends on each method’s feasibility filter (Sec. III-E ), so it is not comparable across methods. Collapses per placement is the number of collapses divided by the number of placement attempts (placed boxes plus collapses) over a method’s 50 evaluation episodes, in percent. An episode has at most one collapse. Thus, within a training seed, if f col f_{\mathrm{col}} is the fraction of episodes ending in collapse and L ¯ \bar{L} is the mean number of successfully placed boxes, collapses per attempt is f col / ( L ¯ + f col ) f_{\mathrm{col}}/(\bar{L}+f_{\mathrm{col}}) before conversion to percent. This normalizes failures by the number of executed attempts; it is not an independent outcome from episode length and unstable rate. It estimates the observed failure frequency under each policy’s visited states, rather than risk on a common set of stacks. A low per-attempt frequency can still accompany frequent episode failures when many placements must succeed in succession.

Stability-model metrics. The ablations (Sec. V-E ) evaluate the learning copy S ψ S_{\psi} on held-out executed outcomes. These outcomes are excluded from supervised training, but simulated labels can cover the same state–action pairs (Sec. IV-D ); the evaluation therefore does not establish generalization to entirely unseen placements. It also does not directly assess the acting copy S ψ ¯ S_{\bar{\psi}} .

AUROC , the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 1 − S ψ 1-S_{\psi} detecting collapses, measures ranking: the probability that a collapsed placement receives a lower prediction than a successful one, with half credit for ties. A score of 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect ranking. This metric opens the activation gate. Expected calibration error (ECE) groups predictions into ten equal-width bins and averages the absolute difference between each bin’s mean prediction and observed success frequency, weighted by bin size. Zero means perfect agreement at this bin resolution. Probability accuracy matters because the critic uses S ψ ¯ S_{\bar{\psi}} multiplicatively, but low ECE does not prove the pointwise accuracy required by Eq. ( 8 ). The metrics are complementary: with rare collapses, a constant high prediction can have low ECE while ranking at chance; good ranking can coexist with pessimistic probabilities. Both metrics use the most recent held-out outcomes after each training iteration: about 4,000, including 37–66 collapses at the reported ablation checkpoint.

Although the box type distribution is shared between training and evaluation (a realistic assumption for a warehouse with standardized box sizes), the arrival order is independently randomized in every evaluation episode, so evaluation sequences are almost surely never seen during training; the combinatorial space of arrival orders is ( 40 10 , 10 , 10 , 10 ) ≈ 4.7 × 10 21 \binom{40}{10,10,10,10}\approx 4.7\times 10^{21} . All metrics are averaged over 50 evaluation episodes with the same fixed episode seeds across all methods, using deterministic (argmax) actions and no search for the learned policies.

Separating action flexibility from stability awareness. The base-set comparison is close to its packing ceiling, while the expanded set tests the method in a more demanding regime: varied geometries constrain future fit, and material properties are independent of shape, so geometry alone cannot identify reliable support. At the base-set checkpoint, GOPT+ has higher utilization and completion than the single-seed SHORE run, despite SHORE’s earlier rise in training reward. The curves therefore suggest faster early learning in this run, not a base-set evaluation advantage or a seed-robust difference. The expanded set provides the stronger test of whether modeling stability helps when box choice, orientation, and future fit interact.

The comparison between GOPT and GOPT+ tests the value of broadening decisions beyond the buffer head and its fixed orientation. GOPT+ is our extension of the official GOPT baseline: it can choose a visible box, its orientation, and an EMS placement, so order, orientation, and location all affect the next packing state. Its stronger performance indicates that exposing these choices can improve packing on the expanded set and supports the importance of flexible, coordinated decisions. This is evidence for the value of the expanded decision space, though the comparison does not isolate action flexibility alone: GOPT+ also uses a different PPO update, with clipped ratios applied separately to item-orientation and placement choices.

Against this stronger diagnostic baseline, SHORE attains higher mean utilization while experiencing fewer collapses both per episode and per placement attempt, despite sharing its action space and actor backbone. The comparison therefore tests what stability-aware valuation and policy guidance add after the joint choices are available. To isolate stability modeling, the relevant control is REPPO-D, which shares the learner but removes both SHORE components. Its eventual utilization matches SHORE within training-seed variation. The evidence thus points to earlier acquisition and a better packing–risk balance, rather than a higher final utilization ceiling.

Why stability supervision helps learning. Figure 4 (a) and the intermediate deterministic checkpoint evaluations show that SHORE reaches its high-utilization regime earlier than the learner without S S . The advantage persists across intermediate checkpoints and appears under both sampled training actions and deterministic evaluation, so it is not merely a consequence of exploration noise in training returns. This pattern supports the hypothesis that separating immediate physical survival from continuation value makes learning easier. Without S S , the critic must infer both effects from returns; a failed placement also removes the opportunity to observe later packing decisions. In SHORE, supervised placement outcomes train a dedicated model with access to the internal density layout, and that information immediately affects the values and probabilities of joint box–orientation–placement choices. The later catch-up of the base learner is consistent with S S supplying useful information sooner, while both ultimately optimize the same packed-volume objective. This learning advantage is measured in rollout environment steps.

Stability without sacrificing useful packing. Table IV shows that SHORE packs more volume than GOPT+ with fewer failures per attempt, while their episode lengths are comparable. Its lower episode-collapse share thus accompanies a lower observed placement failure frequency, rather than simply fewer opportunities to fail. This supports using S S to guide productive joint actions. The two collapse metrics summarize the same failures at different scales; their agreement clarifies the packing–risk trade-off rather than providing independent statistical evidence.

Figure 4 (c) shows how this trade-off develops during learning. After the initial improvement, SHORE sustains fewer collapses per attempt than the learner without S S , alongside higher packed-volume reward in panel (a). GOPT+ approaches its placement-level failure frequency later, consistent with explicit stability supervision accelerating the acquisition of useful physical constraints. OL Mask reveals why both collapse metrics are needed: its failures per attempt decline while its episode-collapse share stays near saturation. It sustains more successful placements before failure, but still fails before completion. Panel (c) therefore reveals progress that panel (b) obscures. These sampled training trajectories complement the deterministic evaluation comparison; they do not measure deployment-policy performance directly.

Balancing stability against packed volume. The expanded set shows two ways to get this trade-off wrong. GOPT is the conservative extreme. It has the lowest observed collapse frequency, yet packs much less volume than the methods that choose from the whole buffer. Its low collapse share is partly a consequence of stopping early: it places only the buffer head in its stored orientation, so most of its episodes end once that box has no admissible placement, after about 41 boxes, and each episode contains fewer placements that could fail. Its restricted actions also make each placement more conservative: it never turns a box onto a smaller face and never packs the last, tightest part of the bin. The training curves show the same regime throughout learning (Fig. 4 ): about 30% of GOPT’s training episodes end in a collapse, the fewest of any method, while its training reward stays near 0.5. GOPT+ is the aggressive counterpart. With buffer selection and rotation it packs more volume, but incurs a higher collapse rate. Because a collapse ends the episode and forfeits every box not yet packed, neither extreme is optimal: avoiding risk leaves space unused, and ignoring risk lets a single failed placement discard the volume the remaining boxes would have added. SHORE’s action value prices this trade-off directly, as the probability that a placement holds times the return if it holds. With the same action space and backbone as GOPT+, it attains higher utilization while experiencing fewer episode collapses and fewer failures per placement. The aim is thus not the lowest collapse rate, which GOPT shows can be bought by stopping early, but the most packed volume for the risk taken. OL Mask fails on both counts: its hard mask admits placements that do not hold, and 99% of its episodes end in a collapse after about 16 boxes, although its different architecture, orientation restriction and training procedure prevent isolating soft versus hard masking as the cause.

No method completes the expanded sequences. For SHORE, fewer collapse endings accompany more geometrically infeasible endings, identifying preservation of usable space and support as a remaining challenge. Its soft prior does not remove geometrically valid actions; earlier choices can nevertheless leave no admissible placement. Infrequent placement failures can still interrupt a long sequence, while avoiding collapse alone does not preserve room for the remaining boxes. Normalization accounts for the number of attempts but not differences in the states visited; establishing lower risk on the same candidate placements would require a separate controlled comparison.

The component and label-source variants are exploratory single-seed comparisons, whereas SHORE and SHORE − - actor prior − - critic weighting average multiple training seeds. Their small differences in packing or collapse share should therefore be treated as directional evidence. The reported metrics describe the learning copy, whereas decisions use the interpolated acting copy. Stability-model metrics also fluctuate across training iterations and are measured on each policy’s own held-out executed outcomes, rather than a common candidate set. They diagnose behavior on the actions each policy encounters; they do not establish uniform accuracy across the joint action space.

Complementary roles of value weighting and the action prior. Table V supports complementary roles for the actor prior and critic weighting: retaining either alone does not recover the full method’s packing performance. Critic weighting makes the value reflect the chance of losing both the current reward and the continuation, but its influence on action selection must pass through actor learning. The prior changes relative action probabilities directly, using voxel information unavailable to the actor, but by itself does not separate survival probability from the critic’s return estimate conditional on survival. Their combination supplies both a physically informed action value and an immediate bias toward actions likely to hold. The observed ordering is consistent with this division of labor, although repeated seeds are needed to establish the interaction reliably.

The CW variant is especially informative: its stability model ranks outcomes at least as well as the full model at the reported checkpoint, yet its packing performance is lower. Prediction quality alone therefore does not explain the full method’s advantage; how the estimate enters decision making matters. This is empirical support for the integration of S S into both modules, rather than evidence that a more accurate classifier automatically yields a better packer. The value factorization in Sec. IV-E supplies the mathematical justification under pointwise accurate stability probabilities and exact mean fitting; these ablations test its practical usefulness with an imperfect learned model. They do not independently validate the stability activation gate or stability trust region, which are retained in the tested variants.

What additional simulated labels contribute. Table VI shows that executed outcomes alone suffice to reach comparable packing performance at the ablation checkpoint. Together with the earlier checkpoint advantage of the default label scheme, this suggests that simulated alternatives mainly help acquire useful stability information before the rollout has supplied enough examples. They are not required to sustain the observed late-stage packing quality. Uncertainty-directed sampling also gives no demonstrated packing advantage over uniform sampling at this budget. The evidence therefore supports the stability model more strongly than it supports a particular acquisition rule or the necessity of extra simulator calls.

The ranking and calibration results explain why more labels need not improve control. The default simulated-label scheme yields stronger outcome ranking but poorer probability calibration than learning from executed outcomes alone. The recorded copy bias provides a plausible mechanism: simulated copies sometimes report collapse where the executed placement holds, pushing S S toward pessimistic probabilities. A ranking metric can improve despite this shift, while the multiplicative critic weighting depends on the probabilities themselves. Conversely, low ECE on mostly successful executed placements need not imply good discrimination of rare failures (Sec. V-C ). These findings support assessing both properties and caution against using either as a surrogate for packing performance. They also identify a concrete improvement path: reduce copy bias and assess label acquisition at matched simulation budgets, while retaining executed outcomes as the calibration reference.

We demonstrate the packing policy on a UFactory Lite6 arm with a vacuum gripper. The system uses a ZED 2i stereo camera and a hand-mounted camera. Fig. 6 shows one illustrated placement sequence. The yellow area serves as the packing bin. The sequence of cubes arrives in the order from right to left. This demonstration shows that our policy can be easily integrated into a robot packing pipeline.

We presented SHORE, an on-policy reinforcement learning method for physics-aware online 3D bin packing, which incorporates learned stability information through a policy prior and continuous weighting of action-conditioned critic values. The experiments support faster acquisition of high-utilization policies than learning without explicit stability modeling. Against GOPT+, which shares the joint action space and actor backbone, SHORE achieves higher mean utilization with fewer collapses per episode and per placement attempt. The training curves further show that the stability model reduces failures per attempt relative to the same learner without it. These findings support using stability information in both action valuation and selection to improve the packing–risk trade-off; the eventual catch-up of the base learner limits claims of a higher final performance ceiling.

Meanwhile, the method is limited by its observation and candidate representations, approximate stability probabilities, and simulator fidelity. A collapse is attributed to the triggering placement even when earlier choices created the fragile structure; those earlier choices receive information only through returns, and the value network cannot see the raw voxel grid of the bin. Collapses per placement account for the number of attempts, but remain specific to the states each policy visits; earlier infeasible termination can prevent exposure to difficult late-stage placements. Stability metrics must therefore be interpreted together with utilization and termination modes. Besides, there are more sim-to-real factors that we did not take into account, such as contact-parameter mismatch, bin wall collisions, and robot reachability.

For future work, it is better to specifically distinguish exogenous factors like incoming box distribution from endogenous factors, and tackle the problem from the exogenous MDP perspective [ 21 ] . Techniques can include, but are not limited to, exogenous state decomposition [ 22 ] or training a predictive model of the exogenous factors.

We used a system-identification-style paired-replay method: identical placement sequences were run in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym, and PhysX parameters were tuned to match per-placement stability verdicts. This increased agreement from 67.0% before calibration to 94.8% after calibration. MuJoCo served as the high-fidelity reference for sim-to-sim transfer; large-scale training and evaluation use Isaac Gym.
